entry.title: Apple's Claris Testing 'Harbor' App for Local AI on Macs (2 minute read)
entry.content:
Harbor is an app currently being tested by Apple's Claris subsidiary that turns Apple Silicon Macs into private AI servers. It supports connecting multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory and enable larger models with higher concurrency. Harbor is in early access and not publicly available. There was an App Store listing, but it has now been removed, so it isn't clear whether the app will be free. The sign-up page for the app asks for a company name, suggesting a business focus.

entry.title: Amazon's Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses (3 minute read)
entry.content:
The Ring Drone Cam is a security camera that can fly from room to room to investigate suspicious activity. For $250, the drone can fly up to eight minutes at a time before autonomously returning to its charging dock. The Ring Rover Cam is a $1,000 device with a display and an extendable periscope camera mounted on a two-wheeled base. The Ring Drone Cam will ship in the US on January 27 (pending approval from the FCC), and the Ring Rover Cam will start shipping on December 16.

entry.title: ‘Flying cars' could launch in China next summer, maker of two-seat model says (4 minute read)
entry.content:

It can be steered using a joystick or fly autonomously to a programmed destination. The price tag includes a six-wheeled van for transporting the vehicle. The flying car has a flight range of 30 kilometers, but XPeng says this will soon be doubled.

entry.title: Q3.5 Timelines Update: Looks Like the Intelligence Explosion Will Happen in 2027 After All (126 minute read)
entry.content:
A Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) is predicted to arrive at some point in 2027, assuming there is no substantial deliberate slowdown in development. AIs that can automate all white-collar work are predicted to arrive before 2028. Companies are currently not on track to align an SAR, and using a misaligned SAR to do recursive self-improvement will have negative consequences. China will probably be able to steal the training recipe and maybe even the model weights if an SAR is trained in the near future.

entry.title: Experimental mRNA therapy promotes repair after heart attack damage (3 minute read)
entry.content:
Researchers have developed a treatment that uses mRNA therapy to reawaken heart muscle cells so that they start to divide and help repair damaged muscle. The treatment helped mice produce stronger heartbeats following a heart attack. While not a full cure for heart disease, even small improvements to heart function have been linked to lower mortality. The treatment is short-lived and localized, and is not expected to cause any permanent modification to the heart cells. Further trials in larger animal models are required before human testing can begin.

entry.title: LLMs are terrible at designing AI systems (6 minute read)
entry.content:
Large language models don't know how to design software that uses LLMs. This could be because most training code is pre-LLMs, or RLVR may just not be a good environment to write code that calls LLMs. Also, current AI agents might just not be good enough at software design for the task. LLMs are good and bad seemingly at random, but if you can predict where they will do well or badly ahead of time, you can get enormous value from them.

entry.title: AI Is Causing Signal Collapse Everywhere All at Once (20 minute read)
entry.content:

We need signals to survive in the modern world, and the rapid collapse of many previously dependable signals will create large shifts in society.

entry.title: They Created a Cell That's Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now? (8 minute read)
entry.content:
A SpudCell is an artificial cell created from lifeless ingredients that can grow, copy its DNA, divide in two, and start its cell cycle all over again. It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.

It is still unclear where the vulnerability resides and what other packages may be vulnerable.
